items.stem: Evaluate Hölzel et al.’s (2011) study of mindfulness and brain grey matter in terms of one strength and one weakness.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The findings suggest that an 8-week programme can change brain regions linked to learning, memory and emotion regulation, which supports using mindfulness to improve well-being. items.answer: (a) The waiting list condition had a higher mean (20.0) than the mindfulness course condition (16.0), suggesting that the mindfulness course reduced stress compared with being on a waiting list. items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Hölzel et al.’s (2011) study of mindfulness and brain grey matter. Include at least one point about the use of MRI.
items.answer: Strength (ethics): MRI is non-invasive, participants gave informed consent, and the control group was offered the MBSR course after the study. Strength (the use of MRI): MRI scans gave objective, quantitative measures of grey matter concentration, so changes in the brain could be measured scientifically rather than inferred from behaviour. Weakness (generalisability): The sample was small (16 in the MBSR group) and consisted of healthy volunteers interested in meditation, so the results may not apply to other people. Weakness (self-report): Home practice time and mindfulness scores were self-reported, so participants may have exaggerated their practice (social desirability). Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss whether psychological interventions can change the structure of the brain. In your answer, you may refer to controls, brain plasticity and usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: Hölzel et al. found increased grey matter concentration in the left hippocampus, posterior cingulate cortex, temporo-parietal junction and cerebellum after MBSR. Give your answers to one decimal place. (b) Calculate the range of scores for each condition. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that adults who complete a mindfulness course will have lower stress scores than adults on a waiting list? Use the data in your answer. (d) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) Mindfulness course: 17.7; waiting list: 22.3. (b) Mindfulness course: 28; waiting list: 11. (c) Mean for mindfulness course = 17.7 and waiting list = 22.3; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 28 and 11) and the sample is small (n = 7 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (d) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.

items.stem: ‘Psychological interventions can change the structure of the brain.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology. In your answer, you may refer to brain plasticity, controls and usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: Hölzel et al. found increased grey matter concentration in the left hippocampus, posterior cingulate cortex, temporo-parietal junction and cerebellum after MBSR. Brain plasticity research shows experience changes neural structure. Arguments against: The sample was small and not randomly allocated. MRI shows correlation with the programme, but other lifestyle changes may have contributed. Changes in grey matter concentration do not necessarily mean changes in behaviour. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
